description: I am a 4th Year Computer Science Student with a hyperfixation on celestial bodies ever since I was a kid and I see this as an opportunity to manifest those. Now with my new skills and knowledge of tools, I want to test myself and see just how far into the stars I can see.
summary:
Talasuri (Tagalog tala, "star", + suri, "to examine") is a free web viewer that turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey into a flipbook of any spot on the sky. You search a name, type coordinates or click the 3D sky sphere. Talasuri then finds every SPHEREx exposure of that position, aligns them on one north-up grid and plays them in time order, so moving and changing objects stand out.

SPHEREx data is public but hard to use without code. One spot is spread across hundreds of large files, every frame sees a different infrared colour, and the pixels are large. Talasuri does that work in the browser. It stacks and subtracts frames, measures a spectrum and light curve, and fits a star's motion from ten years of WISE data. A machine-learning classifier ranks likely moving objects at 84% precision, against 62% for ranking by catalogue signal-to-noise alone.

It matters because nothing like WiseView, the tool citizen scientists used to find cold brown dwarfs in WISE images, existed for SPHEREx. Students get an approachable first view, researchers get measurements they can check against the archive, and the whole interface also works in Filipino.
details:
Talasuri: Project Details

What it does and how it works

Talasuri is a web viewer that shows every NASA SPHEREx infrared image of a chosen spot on the sky as a flipbook, so things that move or change brightness stand out.

  1. Pick a target. Type a name (suggestions come from SIMBAD as you type), type coordinates, or click a spot on the 3D Sky Sphere or in Aladin Lite.
  2. Find the data. The server asks NASA/IPAC's archive (IRSA) which SPHEREx exposures cover that position, across every data release, and removes duplicates.'
  3. Fetch only what is needed. It reads just the needed byte ranges from IRSA's public copy of the archive on Amazon S3, rather than downloading whole files. A first load runs at 5–7 frames per second, against about 0.4–0.75 through IRSA's cutout service. The first frames appear in about 10 seconds, and repeat visits load from cache.
  4. Process each frame. It reads the wavelength at the target, measures the target's brightness on the original pixels, and lines every frame up on one north-up grid.
  5. Show and measure. The browser plays the frames as a flipbook. It can stack frames, subtract a reference image, and plot a spectrum and a light curve.

Three Tabs, for Different Visitors:

Interactive Viewer

For learners and visitors. Displays the flipbook beside a sky map. Pick a position, press play and shows the selected object in the viewer.

Characteristics

For Citizen scientists ans researchers. Displays the technical settings, the image, and measurements (spectrum, light curve, flags, FITS downloads).

Movement Classifier

For those on the lookout. CatWISE2020 sources in the field, ranked by how likely they are to really move.

Special Features

  • WISE motion prediction. Fits a star's position, motion and parallax to its 2010–2024 WISE and NEOWISE detections, then draws the predicted position with its 95% error ellipse on each SPHEREx image. For WISE 0855−0714 the fitted motion is −8132.9 ± 9.1 mas/yr against SIMBAD's −8123.7.
  • Movement Classifier. Gradient-boosted trees, trained on 162,029 sources labelled using Gaia DR3 plus 1,707 known brown-dwarf entries. With whole sky fields held out, it reaches **84% precision** at P ≥ 0.5, against **62%** for ranking by CatWISE motion signal-to-noise alone, and ROC AUC 0.973 against 0.875. It flags 93% of held-out brown dwarfs.

What makes this app really cool

  • No coding needed. Turns hundreds of scattered FITS files into one aligned flipbook in about a minute.
  • Fair comparisons. Every SPHEREx frame sees a different infrared colour. Stacking frames per visit or per detector, and subtracting a reference, keeps colour changes from being mistaken for real ones.
  • Motion becomes visible. Tracking keeps a fast star centred, and difference images show motion as a dark spot next to a bright one.
  • Traceable numbers. Every measurement links back to the original archive file, and the images can be downloaded as FITS.
  • Shareable. Every setting lives in the page address, so a link reproduces the exact view, and `?embed=1` gives a compact player for class pages and articles.

Intended impact

  • Learners start from six worked examples in Help, from Barnard's Star, the fastest-moving star in the sky, to the Orion Nebula, and see motion with one press of play.
  • Citizen scientists get a WiseView-style toolkit for SPHEREx: blinking, difference images, motion fits and a ranked candidate list. WiseView is how volunteers found cold brown dwarfs in WISE images, and nothing like it existed for SPHEREx.
  • Filipino speakers can use the whole interface in their own language, which puts NASA mission data in front of students in the Philippines who read Filipino more comfortably.

Tools and technologies

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy.

Frontend: TypeScript, HTML canvas, Three.js (Sky Sphere), Aladin Lite v3, bundled with esbuild; no UI framework.

Machine learning: scikit-learn for training; the model ships as plain JSON trees evaluated with NumPy.

Data: SPHEREx Spectral Images (NASA/IPAC IRSA, via S3), Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, WISE/NEOWISE, SIMBAD and Sesame (CDS), 2MASS, unWISE/AllWISE, DSS.

Deployment: Runs locally or in Docker; no special hardware.

Testing: 81 backend and 25 frontend automated tests, plus live checks against the archives.

How it is creative

  • A new tool for a new survey. It brings the blink-comparison approach that found brown dwarfs in WISE data to SPHEREx's 102-colour infrared sky.
  • A physical model where it fits, machine learning where it helps. Motion prediction uses a known physical model with error bars that mean what they say. Machine learning is used only where it adds value: telling real motions from artifacts among faint catalogue sources.
  • A star-atlas design. The interface looks like a printed star-atlas plate read under a red night-vision torch. A red ring closes onto the target when its first frame loads, RA/Dec ticks frame the image like a chart, and the science pixels are never tinted.
  • The whole sky as a starting point. A 3D sphere you can view from inside or outside, built from real all-sky maps, lets you choose a target by exploring.

Factors that were considered

Scientific honesty:

  • Images are never altered for display.
  • Brightness values are labelled as quick-look measurements.
  • The app warns when a star is too bright and saturates the detector.
  • It states plainly that a high classifier score is "a reason to look, not a discovery".

Classifier Limits:

  • The classifier is only trained away from the plane of the Milky Way. Its precision for sources Gaia can't see can't be measured. The app shows both limits.

Being polite to the archive:

  • IRSA starts throttling at about 16 parallel requests, so cutouts come from the S3 copy with limited concurrency, and results are cached.

Accesibility:

  • Every control works from the keyboard (Space, arrow keys, D, S, ?).
  • Controls are labelled for screen readers, and keyboard focus is always visible.
  • Text meets WCAG AA contrast.
  • The interface honours reduced-motion settings.
  • On small screens, settings and measurements move into bottom sheets.
  • There is a full Filipino translation, with scientific terms and catalogue names kept in English, as Filipino science writing usually does. A native speaker review is still planned.
  • The SPHEREx, IRSA, Aladin and Gaia acknowledgements are reproduced in full in the app. Talasuri is an independent tool, not an official NASA or IRSA product.

AI Use:

As an individual student, I can only do so much. As a Computer Science Student, Data Science and Machine Learning are my specialties whilst development is my weakness. AI was used in this project to bolster my strengths in Data Science to be able to properly understand the data and for helping me out in development as it is something that I am still dabbling in as of the moment.
